claim: The human brain recurrently prioritizes task-relevant over task-irrelevant visual information.
source: The human brain recurrently prioritizes task-relevant over task-irrelevant visual information.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain function that draws from established scientific understanding of attention and visual processing.

claim: Multivariate classification of electroencephalographic activity allowed tracking of selection of each target separately across time.
source: Multivariate classification of electroencephalographic activity allowed us to track selection of each target separately across time.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study and is supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: There are only small neural and behavioral costs associated with preparing for selecting two objects.
source: The results revealed only small neural and behavioral costs associated with preparing for selecting two objects, but substantial costs when engaging in selection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the behavioral and EEG data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are substantial costs when engaging in selection of two objects.
source: The results revealed only small neural and behavioral costs associated with preparing for selecting two objects, but substantial costs when engaging in selection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the behavioral and EEG data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cost of engaging in selection is the consequence of neural competition resulting in limited parallel processing, rather than a serial bottleneck.
source: Further analyses suggest this cost is the consequence of neural competition resulting in limited parallel processing, rather than a serial bottleneck.
evidence: This is based on inference from the correlation analyses of classifier confidence scores presented in the results.

claim: Attentional templates require the neural activation of task-relevant representations in memory.
source: This requires the neural activation of task-relevant representations in memory – often referred to as attentional templates – which then bias selection towards matching sensory input through top-down recurrent feedback loops (Duncan and Humphreys, 1989; Desimone and Duncan, 1995; Hamker, 2004; Eimer, 2014; Cohen and Tong, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Attentional templates bias selection towards matching sensory input through top-down recurrent feedback loops.
source: This requires the neural activation of task-relevant representations in memory – often referred to as attentional templates – which then bias selection towards matching sensory input through top-down recurrent feedback loops (Duncan and Humphreys, 1989; Desimone and Duncan, 1995; Hamker, 2004; Eimer, 2014; Cohen and Tong, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: There is considerable controversy about whether the brain can enhance multiple task-relevant representations concurrently.
source: A fundamental yet unresolved question is whether the brain can enhance multiple task-relevant representations concurrently – a question that has recently generated considerable controversy, with arguments both for (Houtkamp and Roelfsema, 2009; Menneer et al., 2009; Kristjánsson and Campana, 2010; Dombrowe et al., 2011; Olivers et al., 2011; van Moorselaar et al., 2014; Liu and Jigo, 2017; Ort et al., 2017; Ort et al., 2018; van Driel et al., 2019) and against (Beck et al., 2012; Irons et al., 2012; Grubert and Eimer, 2015; Grubert et al., 2016; Beck and Hollingworth, 2017; Kristjánsson and Kristjánsson, 2017) a strong bottleneck.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on both sides of the debate.

claim: The real bottleneck is not in the number of different templates that can be concurrently active in anticipation of a visual task, but in the number of matching sensory representations that can be enhanced by those templates.
source: We provide electrophysiological evidence showing that the real bottleneck is not so much in the number of different templates that can be concurrently active in anticipation of a visual task, but in the number of matching sensory representations in the incoming signal that can subsequently be enhanced by those templates.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: For the selection of multiple targets to be truly simultaneous, attentional templates need to be set up in memory for each anticipated target feature.
source: Crucially, for the selection of multiple targets to be truly simultaneous, two requirements have to be met. First, attentional templates need to be set up in memory for each anticipated target feature (whether in visual working memory [VWM] or through activating long-term memory [LTM] representations).
evidence: This is a logical requirement stated by the authors based on theoretical considerations.

claim: Multiple representations can be active in memory.
source: Although it is uncontroversial that multiple representations can be active in memory (whether VWM or LTM; e.g., Cowan, 2001), in order to be able to bias selection, each of these representations also needs to be in a state in which it can eventually engage, through recurrent feedback, with matching sensory signals (which is not the same as merely remembering; see Carlisle et al., 2011; Olivers and Eimer, 2011; Kiyonaga et al., 2012; Chatham and Badre, 2015; van Driel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: To simultaneously select multiple targets, the visual system must be able to concurrently use templates to strengthen multiple matching representations in the incoming sensory signal.
source: Second, to simultaneously select multiple targets, the visual system must also be able to concurrently use those templates to strengthen multiple matching representations in the incoming sensory signal.
evidence: This is a logical requirement stated by the authors based on theoretical considerations.

claim: Template activation and template-guided prioritization are distinct processes.
source: It is important to point out that template activation and template-guided prioritization are distinct (cf., Huang and Pashler, 2007): It may be that at any moment multiple templates are ready to potentially engage in the prioritization of visual input, but that only one can actually do so following visual stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and is a key theoretical distinction made in the paper.

claim: Studies of multiple-target selection have only focused on the brain's limits in the readiness to engage in selection, and ignored potential limits in the selection process itself.
source: So far, studies of multiple-target selection have only focused on the brain's limits in the readiness to engage in selection, and ignored potential limits in the selection process itself.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior research that motivates the current study.

claim: Twenty-four participants performed a visual search task requiring them to find two color-defined target characters among distractor characters.
source: Twenty-four participants performed a visual search task for which they were always required to find two color-defined target characters presented among an array of distractor characters, and determine whether these two targets belonged to the same alphanumeric category (see Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: Performance was reliably slower in the 2TMP-1TGT condition than in the 1TMP-1TGT condition (731 ms vs. 679 ms).
source: Specifically, there was an effect of the number of templates on both accuracy and response times, with performance being reliably slower and slightly more error-prone in the 2TMP–1TGT condition than in the 1TMP–1TGT condition (RT: 731 ms vs. 679 ms, t(23) = 5.03, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.64, BF = 572; accuracy: 95.4% vs. 96.5%, t(23) = 2.76, p = 0.01, Cohen's d = 0.61, BF = 4.4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Accuracy was slightly more error-prone in the 2TMP-1TGT condition than in the 1TMP-1TGT condition (95.4% vs. 96.5%).
source: Specifically, there was an effect of the number of templates on both accuracy and response times, with performance being reliably slower and slightly more error-prone in the 2TMP–1TGT condition than in the 1TMP–1TGT condition (RT: 731 ms vs. 679 ms, t(23) = 5.03, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.64, BF = 572; accuracy: 95.4% vs. 96.5%, t(23) = 2.76, p = 0.01, Cohen's d = 0.61, BF = 4.4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Performance was substantially slower in the 2TMP-2TGT condition than in the 2TMP-1TGT condition (916 ms vs. 731 ms).
source: Even stronger costs were observed when the number of uniquely colored targets in the display was increased from one to two, with performance being substantially slower and more error-prone) in the 2TMP–2TGT condition than in the 2TMP–1TGT condition (RT: 916 ms vs. 731 ms, t(23) = 9.05, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.63, BF = 2.5×106; accuracy: 91.4% vs. 95.4%, t(23) = 5.90, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.48, BF = 3.9×103).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Accuracy was more error-prone in the 2TMP-2TGT condition than in the 2TMP-1TGT condition (91.4% vs. 95.4%).
source: Even stronger costs were observed when the number of uniquely colored targets in the display was increased from one to two, with performance being substantially slower and more error-prone) in the 2TMP–2TGT condition than in the 2TMP–1TGT condition (RT: 916 ms vs. 731 ms, t(23) = 9.05, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.63, BF = 2.5×106; accuracy: 91.4% vs. 95.4%, t(23) = 5.90, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.48, BF = 3.9×103).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The engagement cost was greater than the preparation cost on both accuracy and response time measures.
source: Indeed, when we directly compared these two sources of multiple-target cost to each other, the engagement cost was greater than the preparation cost on both measures (accuracy: 4.0% vs. 1.2%, t(23) = 3.36, p = 0.03, Cohen's d = 1.03, BF = 14.8; RT: 185 ms vs. 52 ms, t(23) = 5.00, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.67, BF = 540).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Previous work has shown switch costs, in which selection is slower after the target color changes from one trial to the next trial.
source: Previous work has shown switch costs, in which selection is slower after the target color changes from one trial to the next trial, compared to when the target color stays the same (Maljkovic and Nakayama, 1994; Found and Müller, 1996; Monsell, 2003; Ort et al., 2017; Ort et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Search suffered from switches in terms of response times (repeat trials: 704 ms, switch trials: 754 ms).
source: A closer analysis of the current data also revealed that search suffered from switches, in terms of RTs (repeat trials: M = 704 ms, switch trials: M = 754 ms; t(23) = 8.1, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.56, BFswitchcosts = 4.2×105), and accuracy (repeat trials: M = 95.8%, switch trials: M = 94.9%; t(23) = 2.7, p = 0.01, Cohen's d = 0.40, BFswitchcosts = 4.0).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Search suffered from switches in terms of accuracy (repeat trials: 95.8%, switch trials: 94.9%).
source: A closer analysis of the current data also revealed that search suffered from switches, in terms of RTs (repeat trials: M = 704 ms, switch trials: M = 754 ms; t(23) = 8.1, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.56, BFswitchcosts = 4.2×105), and accuracy (repeat trials: M = 95.8%, switch trials: M = 94.9%; t(23) = 2.7, p = 0.01, Cohen's d = 0.40, BFswitchcosts = 4.0).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Selecting two objects by a single feature is more efficient and more accurate than selecting two objects using two different features.
source: Selecting two objects by a single feature is thus more efficient and more accurate than selecting two objects using two different features.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data presented.

claim: Attentional selection was tracked on both the horizontal and vertical meridian with comparable decoding performance.
source: As a general finding, we were able to track attentional selection on both the horizontal and vertical meridian, with comparable decoding performance.
evidence: This describes the results of the EEG decoding analysis.

claim: The topographical pattern during the early time window (200-350 ms) for the left-right distinction resembles that of the N2pc.
source: For the left-right distinction, the topographical pattern during the early time window (200–350 ms) resembles that of the N2pc, while for later time windows (350–700 ms) it resembles SPCN or CDA-like patterns (Vogel and Machizawa, 2004; Mazza et al., 2007; Grubert and Eimer, 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the observed topographical patterns with known ERP components, supported by citations.

claim: For later time windows (350-700 ms), the topographical pattern resembles SPCN or CDA-like patterns.
source: For the left-right distinction, the topographical pattern during the early time window (200–350 ms) resembles that of the N2pc, while for later time windows (350–700 ms) it resembles SPCN or CDA-like patterns (Vogel and Machizawa, 2004; Mazza et al., 2007; Grubert and Eimer, 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the observed topographical patterns with known ERP components, supported by citations.

claim: Traditional event-related analyses revealed N2pc and SPCN components, which likely contributed to the classifiers' performance.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, more traditional event-related analyses indeed revealed N2pc and SPCN components, which likely contributed to the classifiers' performance.
evidence: This is based on additional ERP analyses shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The decoding approach picks up on information related to attentional selection also on the vertical midline.
source: The fact that the decoding approach picks up on information related to attentional selection also on the vertical midline is testament to its power over conventional ERP methods, and allowed us to simultaneously track attentional selection of both targets over time.
evidence: This is a methodological observation based on the decoding results.

claim: There were no main or interaction effects involving the meridian in any of the comparisons.
source: However, as there were no main or interaction effects involving the meridian in any of the comparisons, we averaged decoding performance across the spatial dimensions.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis.

claim: There was a reliable onset difference between the 1TMP-1TGT (216 ms) and 2TMP-1TGT (237 ms) conditions (21 ms delay).
source: This revealed a reliable onset difference between the 1TMP–1TGT (M = 216 ms) and 2TMP–1TGT (M = 237 ms) conditions (M = 21 ms, tc(23) = 2.21, p = 0.04; Figure 2C), indicating that attentional selection is delayed as a result of having to prepare for two different target colors compared to having to prepare for only a single target color.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG decoding analysis with statistical support.

claim: Attentional selection is delayed as a result of having to prepare for two different target colors compared to having to prepare for only a single target color.
source: This revealed a reliable onset difference between the 1TMP–1TGT (M = 216 ms) and 2TMP–1TGT (M = 237 ms) conditions (M = 21 ms, tc(23) = 2.21, p = 0.04; Figure 2C), indicating that attentional selection is delayed as a result of having to prepare for two different target colors compared to having to prepare for only a single target color.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the onset latency difference observed in the data.

claim: Comparing the onsets between the 2TMP-1TGT (237 ms) and 2TMP-2TGT (263 ms) conditions yielded a further delay of 25 ms associated with having to engage in selecting two target colors.
source: Comparing the onsets between the 2TMP–1TGT (M = 237 ms) and 2TMP–2TGT (M = 263 ms) conditions yielded a further delay of 25 ms associated with having to engage in selecting two target colors compared to selecting a single target color (tc(23) = 2.35, p = 0.03; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG decoding analysis with statistical support.

claim: The onset of the neurophysiological response in the 2TMP-1TGT condition was delayed by 23 ms when the target color switched from one trial to the next, compared to when it repeated.
source: Finally, and also similar to the behavioral responses, the onset of the neurophysiological response in the 2TMP–1TGT condition was delayed by 23 ms when the target color switched from one trial to the next, compared to when it repeated (tc(23) = 4.34, p<0.001; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG decoding analysis with statistical support.

claim: There was an early and short-lasting difference in decoding strength between the 1TMP-1TGT and 2TMP-1TGT conditions, with stronger classification for the single template condition.
source: This procedure revealed an early and short-lasting difference of the number of templates (i.e., between 1TMP–1TGT and 2TMP–1TGT conditions; see Figure 2C), with stronger classification for the single template condition that reflects the onset latency difference reported above.
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster-based permutation test on decoding performance.

claim: More substantial cost in decoding performance emerged when the number of target features in the displays increased from one to two.
source: Again, in line with the behavioral results, more substantial cost in decoding performance emerged when the number of target features in the displays increased from one to two (i.e., between the 2TMP–2TGT and 2TMP–1TGT conditions; see Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster-based permutation test on decoding performance.

claim: The cost of engaging was greater than the cost of preparing selection in a window of 250 to 500 ms post stimulus.
source: To directly compare the cost of preparing two templates to the cost of engaging them in selection, we also ran a cluster-based permutation test on the difference scores (i.e. [2TMP–1TGT – 2TMP–2TGT] – [1TMP–1TGT – 2TMP–1TGT]). This revealed a window of 250 to 500 ms post stimulus in which the cost of engaging was greater than the cost of preparing selection (first cluster: extent: 266–378 ms, p = 0.001; second cluster: extent: 436–495 ms, p = 0.013, results not shown in Figure).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the decoding data.

claim: Generally engaging two templates is more costly than preparing two templates.
source: This suggests that generally engaging two templates is more costly than preparing two templates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical comparison of costs.

claim: Both the onset latency and strength of decoding performance show clear deficits in attentional selection when observers need to select two different targets from a display compared to when they have to select two targets based on the same target color.
source: Thus, both the onset latency and strength of decoding performance show clear deficits in attentional selection when observers need to select two different targets from a display (i.e., engage two templates in selection) compared to when they have to select two targets based on the same target color (i.e., engage one template in selection).
evidence: This is a summary of the decoding results.

claim: Having to set up two templates instead of one came with only minor onset latency differences and no overall differences in decoding strength.
source: In contrast, having to set up two templates instead of one came with only minor onset latency differences and no overall differences in decoding strength.
evidence: This is a summary of the decoding results.

claim: The deficit is when multiple templates need to be engaged simultaneously rather than when multiple templates need to be prepared simultaneously.
source: This clearly points to a deficit when multiple templates need to be engaged simultaneously rather than when multiple templates need to be prepared simultaneously.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of results.

claim: A serial model predicts that attention to a target on one dimension should go at the expense of attention to the target on the other dimension, and thus decoding performance for the vertical and horizontal axes to correlate negatively.
source: A serial model predicts that attention to a target on one dimension should go at the expense of attention to the target on the other dimension, and thus decoding performance for the vertical and horizontal axes to correlate negatively.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction used to test competing models.

claim: In case of parallel, independent selection, there should be no systematic relationship between classification confidence for one dimension and classification confidence for the other dimension.
source: In case of parallel, independent selection, there should be no systematic relationship between classification confidence for one dimension and classification confidence for the other dimension, as selection of one target is impervious to the selection of the other target.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction used to test competing models.

claim: A positive correlation would arise from a common mechanism driving selection of two different targets.
source: A positive correlation would arise from a common mechanism driving selection of two different targets.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction used to test competing models.

claim: There was no systematically positive or negative relationship in the correlation of classification performance over time for individual participants (average correlation Spearman's ρ = 0.11).
source: Although this revealed incidental positive and negative correlations for individual participants, there was no systematically positive or negative relationship (average correlation Spearman's ρ = 0.11; min-max range: −0.37–0.63; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis at the individual participant level.

claim: There was no systematic relationship between decoding the locations of the two targets in any of the conditions at the trial level.
source: As can be seen, there was again no systematic relationship between decoding the locations of the two targets, in any of the conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the trial-level correlation analysis of classifier confidence scores.

claim: Apart from a short-lasting positive correlation around the 500 ms time point in the 2TMP-2TG condition, which is likely to be spurious, correlations for all time points were close to zero.
source: Apart from a short-lasting positive correlation around the 500 ms time point in the 2TMP–2TG condition, which is likely to be spurious, correlations for all time points were close to zero, which implies that classifying horizontal and vertical target positions is independent from each other.
evidence: This is a finding from the trial-level correlation analysis with interpretation.

claim: Classifying horizontal and vertical target positions is independent from each other.
source: Apart from a short-lasting positive correlation around the 500 ms time point in the 2TMP–2TG condition, which is likely to be spurious, correlations for all time points were close to zero, which implies that classifying horizontal and vertical target positions is independent from each other.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation results.

claim: With sufficiently high decoding AUC values (>approx. 0.55-0.60), correlations (whether positive or negative) between the horizontal and vertical position classifiers can, in principle, be reliably detected.
source: The results of this simulation are summarized in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and demonstrate that with sufficiently high decoding AUC values (>approx. 0.55–0.60), correlations (whether positive or negative) between the horizontal and vertical position classifiers can, in principle, be reliably detected.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis.

claim: Even for individuals with relatively high classification scores, there was no evidence for a correlation between the classification confidence between the two target dimensions.
source: As Figure 3B shows, even for individuals with relatively high classification scores, there was no evidence for a correlation between the classification confidence between the two target dimensions.
evidence: This is a finding from the individual-level analysis at peak decoding performance.

claim: The absence of correlation in the data is most consistent with a limited parallel independent selection model, rather than a serial model or a parallel model operating under a common mechanism.
source: The absence of such a correlation in our data is thus most consistent with a limited parallel independent selection model, rather than a serial model or a parallel model operating under a common mechanism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the null result from the correlation analyses.

claim: The conclusion that the data are mostly consistent with a limited parallel model is based on a null result and therefore has to be interpreted with care.
source: We emphasize that the conclusion that our data are mostly consistent with a limited parallel model is thus based on a null result and therefore has to be interpreted with care.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of the results.

claim: Limitations in visual selection do not so much reside at the level of template preparation but at the extent to which templates can be concurrently engaged in selecting matching information from the sensory input.
source: The current results provide evidence that these limitations do not so much reside at the level of template preparation (i.e., the number of target representations set up prior to the task), but at the extent to which templates can then be concurrently engaged in selecting matching information from the sensory input.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental results.

claim: Relatively small but reliable costs were observed on both behavioral and EEG classification performance when two templates needed to be activated instead of one.
source: Specifically, we observed relatively small but reliable costs on both behavioral and EEG classification performance when two templates needed to be activated instead of one, suggesting a reliable but relatively minor bottleneck at this stage of processing.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings regarding template preparation costs.

claim: Substantial costs emerged on both behavioral and EEG performance measures when two templates had to be prepared, and both of these templates had to be engaged in driving the selection of two different targets.
source: In contrast, substantial costs emerged on both behavioral and EEG performance measures when two templates had to be prepared, and both of these templates (rather than just one) had to be engaged in driving the selection of two different targets.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings regarding template engagement costs.

claim: The activation of target templates in memory involves the pre-activation or biasing of associated sensory features.
source: According to these frameworks, the activation of target templates in memory involves the pre-activation or biasing of associated sensory features.
evidence: This is a description of existing theoretical frameworks.

claim: The presence of target features in the input will trigger a long-range recurrent feedback loop, leading to the enhancement of the target representation in VWM.
source: The presence of such features in the input will then trigger a long-range recurrent feedback loop, leading the enhancement of the target representation in VWM (including its location), and thus making it available for other cognitive processes such as response selection (processes which are themselves limited, cf. Dehaene et al., 1998; Lamme, 2003; Baars, 2005).
evidence: This is a description of existing theoretical frameworks with citations.

claim: While multiple top-down feedback connections may be prepared at once, there is a limitation in how these feedback loops are engaged by matching input.
source: Our data indicates that while multiple top-down feedback connections may be prepared at once, there is a limitation in how these feedback loops are engaged by matching input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Multiple templates may hold each other in a mutually competitive relationship in memory, most likely through laterally suppressive connections.
source: Specifically, we propose that multiple templates may hold each other in a mutually competitive relationship in memory, most likely through laterally suppressive connections (Manohar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the findings, with citation to support the mechanism.

claim: If only one target feature is present, the corresponding template will automatically win the competition.
source: If only one target feature is present, the corresponding template will automatically win the competition.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model explaining the results.

claim: Although two templates can be maintained in parallel, the mutual competition between them is slightly disadvantageous.
source: Although two templates can be maintained in parallel, the mutual competition between them is slightly disadvantageous.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model explaining the results.

claim: The mutual competition between templates will lead to the initial delay in target selection that was observed when two templates instead of just one were activated.
source: This will lead to the initial delay in target selection that we observed in the data when two templates instead of just one were activated.
evidence: This is an explanation of the observed delay based on the proposed model.

claim: The selective enhancement of one representation over another may carry over to the next trial, thus resulting in the target switch costs.
source: Moreover, the selective enhancement of one representation over another may carry over to the next trial, thus resulting in the target switch costs that we also observed both in behavior and EEG performance measures.
evidence: This is an explanation of the switch costs based on the proposed model.

claim: When both templates are activated, the mutual suppression will prevent strong activation of either, resulting in substantially weakened and delayed selection of both targets.
source: Because of the mutually suppressive relationship, strengthening one feedback loop will automatically go at the expense of the other. Although both loops are triggered in parallel, the mutually aversive relationship results in slower and weaker accumulation of evidence for either of the targets, consistent with what we observed in the data.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model explaining the results when both templates are engaged.

claim: The system may resolve competition by keeping selection of both targets running in parallel and accepting the slower evidence accumulation.
source: In theory, the system may resolve such competition in two ways. The first is to keep selection of both targets running in parallel, and accept the slower evidence accumulation.
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility discussed by the authors.

claim: The system may resolve competition by imposing a serial strategy in which selection is first biased in favor of one target, and then switched to the other.
source: The second option is to impose a serial strategy in which selection is first biased in favor of one target, and then switched to the other (or alternate between the two).
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility discussed by the authors.

claim: The data provides no evidence for the serial model.
source: Our data provides no evidence for the serial model.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation analyses.

claim: The average group data nor the average individual subject data showed any systematic pattern of switching between the two target positions.
source: First, the average group data nor the average individual subject data showed any systematic pattern of switching between the two target positions (i.e., differences in classification performance for left-right versus top-bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of decoding performance.

claim: A trial-based correlation analysis of classifier confidence scores showed the absence of a negative correlation between the target positions.
source: Second, also a trial-based correlation analysis of classifier confidence scores showed the absence of a negative correlation between the target positions.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: The findings are most consistent with a limited-capacity parallel model, in which observers maintain two templates active during search, but with mutually aversive consequences.
source: Our findings are therefore most consistent with a limited-capacity parallel model, in which observers maintain two templates active during search, but with mutually aversive consequences.
evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion based on the pattern of results.

claim: The data do not exclude the possibility of seriality.
source: However, we point out that our data do not exclude the possibility of seriality.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of the results.

claim: While there may have been little seriality in selecting the targets from the displays on the basis of color, there may have been a serial component in accessing their alphanumeric identity.
source: First, while there may have been little seriality in selecting the targets from the displays on the basis of color, there may have been a serial component in accessing their alphanumeric identity — a component to which our classifier was not sensitive.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential limitations of the study.

claim: Imposing seriality is a valid strategy that observers may deploy to resolve competition between different target features, but such choices depend on tasks, context, or instructions.
source: Moreover, there is still a distinct possibility that imposing seriality is a valid strategy that observers may deploy to resolve competition between different target features, but that such choices depend on tasks, context, or instructions (Cave et al., 2018; Stroud et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Evidence for serial switching was previously observed in a different paradigm when observers had to select only one of two targets present, and were instructed to switch at least a few times during a block.
source: For example, we previously observed evidence for serial switching in a different paradigm when observers had to select only one of two targets present, and were instructed to switch at least a few times during a block (Ort et al., 2019; van Driel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research by the authors.

claim: The current results indicate that the process can occur in parallel, not that it must.
source: The current results indicate that the process can occur in parallel, not that it must.
evidence: This is a clarification of what the results demonstrate.

claim: The account has a resemblance to the Boolean Map Theory of Visual Attention.
source: Our account has a resemblance to the Boolean Map Theory of Visual Attention (Huang and Pashler, 2007), which proposes a division of attentional selection into two components: (1) The feature-to-location routine, in which task-relevant features are being located in the visual field (referred to by Huang and Pashler as selection, but here analogous to what we call preparation for selection) and (2) the location-to-feature routine in which individuals extract response-relevant features at a target location (access, analogous to what we here call engagement in selection).
evidence: This is a comparison to an existing theoretical framework with citation.

claim: In contrast to the proposed model, the Boolean Map theory poses a capacity limitation of one on both selection and access.
source: However, in contrast to the model that we propose, in which only what Huang and Pashler refer to as the access aspect of search is severely limited, the Boolean Map theory poses a capacity limitation of one on both selection and access.
evidence: This is a comparison highlighting differences between the proposed model and an existing theory.

claim: The distinction between template preparation and template engagement in selection has great potential for resolving the current debate on whether observers can look for more than a single target at the same time.
source: We believe the distinction between template preparation and template engagement in selection has great potential for resolving the current debate on whether observers can look for more than a single target at the same time (Menneer et al., 2009; Beck et al., 2012; Irons et al., 2012; Grubert and Eimer, 2015; Beck and Hollingworth, 2017; Ort et al., 2017; Ort et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a claim about the theoretical contribution of the work, with citations to the relevant debate.

claim: Studies central to the debate have largely focused on how many templates can be prepared in anticipation for a search, rather than how many of these templates can then be concurrently engaged in selection without costs.
source: Studies central to this debate have largely focused on how many templates can be prepared in anticipation for a search, rather than how many of these templates can then be concurrently engaged in selection without costs.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior research.

claim: Observers may look for multiple targets simultaneously at little cost, but it is selecting those targets that runs into real limitations.
source: From our data, the answer to the question then appears to be yes, observers may look for multiple targets simultaneously at little cost, but it is selecting those targets that runs into real limitations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Costs will likely increase more strongly with more templates being added beyond two.
source: Although we found the costs of going from one to two templates to be relatively small, this leaves open the question whether costs will increase more strongly with more templates being added.
evidence: This is speculation about what might happen with additional templates.

claim: The capacity of VWM is thought to be around three to four items for colored shapes.
source: Although the capacity of VWM is thought to be around three to four items (at least for the standard colored shapes used in experiments like ours), and VWM is assumed to be central to top-down driven search, there is ample evidence that visual search needs not solely rely on VWM.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: There is ample evidence that visual search need not solely rely on VWM.
source: Although the capacity of VWM is thought to be around three to four items (at least for the standard colored shapes used in experiments like ours), and VWM is assumed to be central to top-down driven search, there is ample evidence that visual search needs not solely rely on VWM.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: Given that in the experiment the target template remained the same for a block of trials, observers may have at least partly relied on trained templates in long term memory.
source: In fact, given that in our experiment the target template remained the same for a block of trials, observers may have at least partly relied on trained templates in long term memory here (Carlisle et al., 2011; Gunseli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about the memory system used, supported by citations.

claim: Observers can successfully search for any one of tens of different target objects if given the opportunity to first commit these objects to long term memory.
source: Moreover, work by Wolfe (2012) has shown that observers can successfully search for any one of tens of different target objects if given the opportunity to first commit these objects to long term memory.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Effects of capacity limits and interference may have been stronger when the targets would have been cued from trial to trial, rather than from block to block.
source: In our study, effects of capacity limits and any interference arising from it may be have been stronger when the targets would have been cued from trial to trial, rather than from block to block.
evidence: This is speculation about how the design might have affected the results.

claim: The fact that limitations are found even with repeated targets is testament to the mechanistic bottleneck in the engagement of selection.
source: Conversely, the fact that we find limitations even with repeated targets is testament to the mechanistic bottleneck in the engagement of selection that we propose.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in light of the experimental design.

claim: Even LTM representations would need to become activated for effective task-or context-driven guidance.
source: One reason may be that even LTM representations would need to become activated for effective task-or context-driven guidance (since only one set of trained colors is relevant in a particular block).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed limitations.

claim: The limit may well be in the goal-driven aspect of search – that is, the deployment of a representation for perceptual bias rather than its storage per se.
source: Our data suggests that the limit may well be in this goal-driven aspect of search – that is, the deployment of a representation for perceptual bias rather than its storage per se.
evidence: This is an interpretation of where the bottleneck occurs based on the findings.

claim: Attentional selection per se, as measured by the N2pc, is not affected by whether targets are stored in long term memory or working memory.
source: In line with this, Grubert et al. (2016) reported evidence that attentional selection per se, as measured by the N2pc (which at least partly underlies the signal also used here), is not affected by whether targets are stored in long term memory or working memory.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Current limitations were found when both target features were drawn from the same dimension (color).
source: Finally, the question of memory capacity or interference is also important when considering that current limitations were found when both target features were drawn from the same dimension (color).

claim: There is evidence that different dimensions may to some extent independently store or guide attention towards target features.

claim: Models of visual selection need to consider the difference between preparing for selection and engaging in selection of multiple visual targets.
source: To sum up, we propose that models of visual selection need to consider the difference between preparing for selection and engaging in selection of multiple visual targets.
evidence: This is the main theoretical proposal of the paper.

claim: The first process (preparing for selection) comes at little cost, while the true bottleneck of multiple-target selection is in engaging multiple template representations.
source: We demonstrate that whereas the first process comes at little cost, the true bottleneck of multiple-target selection is in engaging multiple template representations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Thirty-two participants naive to the purpose of the experiment were recruited.

claim: Eight participants were excluded due to poor behavioural performance in at least one experimental condition (accuracy <85%).
source: Eight were excluded due to poor behavioural performance in at least one experimental condition (a predefined cutoff of accuracy <85% was used, see below) to ensure sufficient numbers of correct trials for the EEG analyses.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria applied in the study.

claim: The N2pc is an event-related potential characterized by increased negativity over posterior electrodes contralateral to the hemifield in which the target is located.
source: Traditionally, visual target selection is assessed using the N2pc, an event-related potential (ERP) in the EEG signal that is characterized by increased negativity over posterior electrodes contralateral to the hemifield in which the target is located (Luck and Hillyard, 1994; Eimer, 1996).
evidence: This is a description of an established EEG component, supported by citations.

claim: The N2pc can only distinguish between the left versus right hemifield and is not able to simultaneously track the selection of multiple targets at different locations in complex visual search displays.
source: However, because the N2pc can only distinguish between the left versus right hemifield, it is not able to simultaneously track the selection of multiple targets at different locations in more complex visual search displays.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the N2pc method.

claim: Multivariate decoding has been proven to successfully track the spatiotemporal dynamics of feature-based selection processes at any location in a search display.
source: To overcome this limitation, we used multivariate decoding, which has been proven to successfully track the spatiotemporal dynamics of feature-based selection processes at any location in a search display (Fahrenfort et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.
